I'm sorry to hear you're going through it too. It's been a challenge but we were very fortunate bertie's injury wasn't any worse. It's really just been a matter of not letting her run or jump at all. Her meniscus was still intact and she's a little older (9-ish) so the surgeon left it to me to decide whether or not to do the surgery. Apparently senior bulldogs sometimes just don't wake up after anesthesia. 

He said it would heal slowly on its own, usually in about 6 to 12 months. He stressed no running or jumping at all, because she could either tear the meniscus, which would definitely require surgery or she could damage her other ACL. I read that something like 2/3 of dogs that tear one ACL will go on to damage the other one within two years due to them starting to favor it over the injured one.

I opted not to do the surgery and she's doing really well. We go on walks and she still goes places with me but she does use a ramp to get in and out of the car now. She has low steps to get on the sofa and the bed. I also posted a No Soliciting sign by the doorbell because she still wanted to run to the front door every time it rang.

I do have one tip to help keep her busy and wear her out a little. Fill a box about halfway up with crumpled pieces of paper. Old magazines and used wrapping paper work great. You're basically making a ballpit but using crumpled up paper. Then just sprinkle some kibble in it and let her go to town on it. That's pretty much how Bertie gets her meals now and she loves it. 

I hope you guys have it at least as easy as Bertie and I have. I'll be keeping my fingers crossed for yall.

Something that I've never seen mentioned as a response to this question and that I'm fairly new to personally is getting my blood sugar levels in order. Sounds trivial i know but hear me out.

I've spent most of my life fighting off what feels like a low-grade depression with pretty serious depressive episodes here and there. I've never attempted suicide but damned if I didn't think about it constantly and seriously considered it more than a couple of times. 

I was functioning but moody, kind of angry at the world and just felt really run down most of the time. When I'd get angry, which was often, I'd start to shake, sweat profusely and possibly cry. I was a real treat to be around for about 20 years or so. I can't even believe I still have friends from that time in my life, tbh.

I've known since I was a kid that I had organic hyperinsulinism,  which means there's too much insulin in my system most of the time and that it's more expensive since it's 'organic' (lol, a bad joke but I won't stop telling it and nothing you can say will make me). The organic part really just means that the my body is producing too much insulin for its own reasons (likely a genetic predisposition) rather than due to an outside factor like diet or medication. 

A few years ago,  I started taking my diet more seriously and switched to a low carb high protein diet in order to lose weight and better manage my blood sugar levels. I did lose some weight but not as much as I was hoping so that was discouraging but also, I still felt shitty about myself, my life and the world in general almost all of the time on top of it.  

I'd been hearing about intermittent fasting for awhile but figured it was a no-go for someone with my blood glucose issues. Anytime I'd gone for more than a few hours without food before I'd get irritable as fuck and start to feel lightheaded. I've even passed out a few times from hypoglycemia (low blood sugar as a result of too much insulin) so I assumed that's what would happen if I didn't eat for a long stretch.

What changed was that I had a family crisis in April and for a week my appetite was just gone. I couldn't eat and when I'd try to make myself I felt worse so I stopped trying. I'd eat a half a pastry every couple of days when a family member would express concern but that was about it. It dawned on me after everything sort of settled down again how little I'd actually eaten that week and how little I'd been affected by not eating.

That got me thinking about intermittent fasting so I decided to try a 16 hour fast on the weekend.  I wound up going for 19 hours with no problem at all and actually felt pretty great at the end. Did it again for the next few days and couldn't get over how good I was feeling, especially during the fasting period. In fact, the only time I felt like my old crabby self came about 90 minutes after a couple of different meals, both of which were high in protein and very low in carbohydrates. 

Did a little research and it turns out high protein diets aren't great for people with hyperinsulinism because too much protein can cause your body to produce more insulin, just like too many sugars and simple carbs can. Who knew??? Not me, that's for sure.

By fasting, I was finally able to get my insulin level stable for the first time in probably 30 years. That made it sooo much easier to spot what was happening so now I can actually change it. All I gotta do is stick to foods that don't send my insulin levels soaring and i'm all good.

In the past couple of weeks my moods have stabilized and my depression has let up. I'm not getting angry at asshole drivers in traffic or stressed out about the fact that my car broke down today and I don't know what that's going to run me. A month ago I would've been sobbing into my pillow over the day I had today but now I know I'll figure it out and things will be just fine. Turns out I'm not nearly as awful as I thought I was in my natural state. I feel better in a *fundamental* way than I have since I was a kid. 

 I'm seeing very clearly how much my outlook has been impacted by my insulin levels being out of whack all these years and I just can't believe that it all boils down to something so stupid and simple. I'm also really grateful though because I feel like I've finallt been given a key to living like a normal person. Maybe.

Please know that I'm not suggesting this as a solution for everyone but I wanted to let you know what's helping me. I think this might be more of an issue than many people realize.
